skill.name: hypothesis-generation
skill.description: Helps researchers generate evidence-based, testable hypotheses, compare competing explanations, design experiments, and produce structured LaTeX reports.
skill.summary: Generate evidence-based hypotheses with predictions, experiments, quality checks, and report structure.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown backticks, LaTeX commands, research guidance, or PubMed search examples. Confirmed risks are limited to explicit Bash workflows for schematic generation and LaTeX compilation, plus a medium-confidence concern about an unbundled external schematic dependency.

remediation.issue: External command execution is part of the documented workflow.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user confirmation before running python, xelatex, or bibtex commands, and explain what files they read or write.

remediation.issue: The mandatory schematic workflow references an external skill and a missing script.
remediation.suggestion: Bundle the script, remove the mandatory requirement, or clearly document the separate dependency and its trust boundary.

remediation.issue: Literature searches may disclose sensitive research terms to external services.
remediation.suggestion: Add a privacy note and ask users before using WebFetch, WebSearch, or PubMed URLs for confidential topics.

content.value_statement: Researchers need rigorous hypotheses, predictions, and experiments from limited observations. This skill structures literature search, competing explanations, quality checks, and LaTeX-style reports for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
actual_capabilities: Turns observations or research questions into three to five competing scientific hypotheses.
Guides PubMed and general literature searches to ground hypotheses in existing evidence.
Evaluates hypotheses for testability, falsifiability, parsimony, explanatory power, scope, consistency, and novelty.
Proposes experiments, controls, measurements, confounds, and study designs for each viable hypothesis.
Formats outputs as concise main text with appendices using bundled LaTeX templates and style guidance.
Defines testable predictions that distinguish competing mechanisms.
limitations: It does not validate scientific truth or replace expert peer review.
It depends on current literature access for strong evidence synthesis.
Its schematic generation workflow references a separate skill and script not included in this package.
LaTeX compilation requires local XeLaTeX, BibTeX, and required packages.

use_cases.title: Plan a Thesis Study
use_cases.description: Convert an early research observation into competing mechanisms, predictions, and initial experiments.

use_cases.title: Shape a Grant Proposal
use_cases.description: Build evidence-based hypotheses, define key controls, and identify decisive experiments for a proposal.

use_cases.title: Explore Product Research Signals
use_cases.description: Turn experimental results into plausible causal explanations and practical next tests.

prompt_templates.title: Start from an Observation
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner hypothesis generation from a single phenomenon.
prompt_templates.prompt: Generate three testable hypotheses for this observation: [observation]. Include a short mechanism, key prediction, and one experiment for each.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Competing Explanations
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate evaluation of several possible mechanisms.
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare these hypotheses for [phenomenon]: [hypotheses]. Evaluate testability, falsifiability, parsimony, evidence, and decisive predictions.

prompt_templates.title: Design Experiments
prompt_templates.prompt: Design experiments to test this hypothesis: [hypothesis]. Include controls, measurements, sample considerations, confounds, and expected outcomes.

prompt_templates.title: Build a Full Hypothesis Report
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a structured hypothesis report for [research question]. Include literature synthesis, competing hypotheses, predictions, experimental designs, limitations, and appendices.

output_examples.input: Observation: A biomarker rises before symptoms appear in a disease cohort.
output_examples.output: A report with competing causal, compensatory, and correlated-marker hypotheses, each paired with predictions and validation studies.

output_examples.input: Question: Why does an intervention help one subgroup but not another?
output_examples.output: A ranked set of mechanistic explanations, subgroup-specific predictions, required controls, and experiments to separate biology from measurement bias.

output_examples.input: Need: Convert a literature gap into a proposal-ready research plan.
output_examples.output: A concise hypothesis framework with evidence summary, experimental design options, risks, and appendix-ready supporting details.

best_practices: Provide the observation, domain, known constraints, and any preliminary data before asking for hypotheses.
Ask for competing hypotheses, not only the most likely explanation.
Review generated citations, mechanisms, and experiments with a qualified domain expert.
anti_patterns: Do not treat generated hypotheses as proven facts.
Do not skip falsifying predictions or negative controls.
Do not run external commands or web searches without checking privacy and local execution risks.

faq.question: What does this skill generate?
faq.answer: It generates competing hypotheses, predictions, quality checks, experimental designs, and structured report guidance.

faq.question: Can it search the literature?
faq.answer: It guides PubMed and web search strategies when the host tool allows web access.

faq.question: Does it prove a hypothesis is correct?
faq.answer: No. It helps design testable ideas, but evidence and expert review remain required.

faq.question: What outputs can I expect?
faq.answer: You can expect concise main findings, detailed appendices, predictions, experimental tests, and LaTeX-oriented formatting.

faq.question: Does it require external tools?
faq.answer: Some workflows reference web search, schematic generation, and LaTeX compilation. These depend on your local environment.

faq.question: Who should use it?
faq.answer: Researchers, students, and applied teams can use it to plan studies and compare explanations.
